pending_articles.title: SAIL: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Alignment of Human Vision and Multimodal Large Language Models
pending_articles.content: Alignment between human high-level visual representations and those of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a quantitative framework for understanding information processing in human vision. However, similarities between model and brain representations do not directly reveal the semantic content underlying their correspondence, as this content is difficult to isolate in entangled MLLM representations. Here, we introduce SAIL, an interpretable framework that formulates voxel interpretation as a multi-unit sparse semantic correspondence problem between MLLMs and human vision. First, we train unified cross-layer sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on MLLM representations of Natural Scenes Dataset images and captions, and align each brain voxel with multiple SAE units. Second, we quantify semantic similarity between their top-response image sets to map semantic alignment across the cortex. We project multiple semantic labels back onto the cortex to interpret the content of this alignment. Finally, we assess these correspondences using category responses measured in independent fLoc experiments. Compared with SAEs trained independently at each layer, SAIL exhibits lower redundancy in SAE unit response profiles and higher semantic alignment. We find that semantic alignment is organized along the human ventral visual pathway across the models and subjects examined. The projected labels reveal semantic preferences within canonical visual regions, while fLoc experiments show agreement between predicted and measured category response patterns. Exploratory analyses further reveal cortical distributions of action-related semantics consistent with established functional accounts of lateral occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortex. Overall, SAIL provides an interpretable account of the semantic correspondences between MLLM representations and human visual responses.

pending_articles.title: Netrin signaling shapes sexually dimorphic neurite branching of a sex-shared interneuron in C. elegans
pending_articles.content: Sexually dimorphic behaviors arise from underlying differences in neural circuit architecture between the sexes, yet the molecular mechanisms that establish these structural differences remain poorly understood. In Caenorhabditis elegans, the sex-shared interneuron AVG exhibits sexually dimorphic synaptic connectivity, offering a model for investigating the development of sexually dimorphic neuronal morphology. Here, we identified that AVG displays male-specific neurite branching and demonstrated that the conserved axon guidance cue UNC-6/Netrin and its receptor UNC-40/DCC are essential for this structural remodeling. Cell-specific manipulation of sexual identity revealed that male identity confers branching competence to AVG. Loss of UNC-6 or UNC-40 abolished branch formation, whereas loss of the alternate Netrin receptor UNC-5/Unc5 had no detectable effect. Cell-specific rescue experiments showed that UNC-40 functions in AVG through its UNC-6 binding domains. Furthermore, genetic ablation of the male-specific presynaptic neuron PCA, which expresses unc-6, diminished AVG branch length, establishing PCA as a candidate local source of UNC-6. Together, our findings support a model in which presynaptic UNC-6/Netrin cues from male-specific neurons promote dimorphic neurite branching in sex-shared neurons, illustrating how evolutionarily conserved signaling molecules are redeployed during sexual maturation to sculpt sex-specific neural circuits.

pending_articles.title: On-demand surround suppression explains the spatiotemporal window of the tilt illusion
pending_articles.content: What we see at one location depends on what surrounds it. Such contextual e[ff]ects are thought to arise from neural signals that travel across the retinotopic representations.Because these signals need more time to travel longer distances, a more distant surround should influence perception most strongly when presented earlier, compensating for its delay. We tested this prediction in human observers using a visual illusion in which a central target appears tilted away from the orientation of its surround (tilt illusion). Measuring the temporal window of this illusion using psychophysical reverse correlation revealed the opposite: the most e[ff]ective surround occurred progressively later as distance increased. Computational modelling demonstrated that this reversal is explained if the visual system sends out a query that recruits contextual information on demand. Perceptual appearance may thus be constructed through temporally unfolding interactions in which context is actively gathered, not passively received.
pending_articles.author: Nakamura, T., Okubo, L., Miyoshi, K., Murakami, I.

pending_articles.title: Facial color properties affect perceived age.
pending_articles.content: Age is a fundamental social attribute that affects rights, responsibilities and even social status. Color information of the face can affect perceived age, but the nature of its contribution, independent of luminance information, remains underexplored. To better characterize the role of color in age perception, we conducted two experiments. In our first experiment, we tested whether natural age-related changes in facial color alone can drive changes in perceived age. In our second experiment, we manipulated red-green contrast across faces aged 18-91 and tested the effect of this manipulation of perceived youthfulness. Our findings demonstrate that natural age-related color changes do provide cues for age perception, dissociable from luminance information. We also found that the optimal red-green contrast level to make faces look the youngest was significantly higher than the originals, meaning that faces tended to appear younger when their redness was accentuated, even though average face redness increases with age. Our analysis revealed that younger faces required greater increases in redness level compared to their older counterparts to achieve the youngest appearance. These results suggest that the spatial distribution of redness contributes to apparent youthfulness, especially in younger faces.

pending_articles.title: Resolution-aware spectral parameterization reveals robust context-dependent aperiodic EEG dynamics during real-world table tennis
pending_articles.content: Mobile EEG can link neuroimaging to natural behavior, but effects recorded during movement, and sport in particular, are difficult to interpret because neural activity overlaps with signals from movement, muscle activity, and cable movement artifacts. We analyzed the OpenNeuro Real World Table Tennis dataset to test whether peri-hit spectral activity could be analyzed and how it differed between human-opponent and ball-machine play. Data from 25 participants comprising EEG, noise-layers, EMG and motion recordings was analyzed with pre-hit, impact, and post-hit windows. EEG power bands were residualized using trial-level root mean square from noise-layer, EMG, and motion/miscellaneous channels. Spectral parameterization modeled spectra as an aperiodic component plus periodic peaks. The principal short-window model was resolution-aware; sensitivity analyses reduced model complexity, used a 2.0-s peri-hit subwindow (-1.0 to +1.0 s), or disabled periodic fitting. Results showed residualized alpha and beta power was lower during ball-machine play, including pre-hit posterior alpha power. The clearest context difference was a higher ball-machine aperiodic exponent over posterior and parietal sensors, corresponding to a steeper broadband spectral slope. Posterior post-hit means were 0.451 and 0.606 for human-opponent and ball-machine play, respectively. A focal parietal effect persisted across specifications. The results support artifact-informed, resolution-aware spectral analysis as an effective approach for detecting robust spectral differences between naturalistic visuomotor contexts and suggest that EEG may provide useful information about the processes engaged by different practice environments, without establishing a single cognitive or physiological mechanism or demonstrating a training outcome.
pending_articles.author: Guchait, A., Chen, C.-Y., Muggleton, N. G.

pending_articles.title: A comprehensive physiological dataset of pain and aversive modalities for pain biomarkers research
pending_articles.content: While progress has been made in identifying pain biomarkers using neuroimaging, the development of reliable EEG-based biomarkers remains challenging, limited by small sample sizes and the lack of adequate control conditions. We present a comprehensive dataset from 125 pain-free adults, comprising electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, and behavioural, sociodemographic, and psychological data. Galvanic skin response and electrocardiogram data were also recorded in a subset of participants (n = 76). Participants received two sustained painful stimulations (thermal, chemical) and two sustained aversive non-painful stimulations (auditory, taste), each delivered twice (with and without continuous intensity ratings). Data are provided in Brain Imaging Data Structure format, where all physiological, stimulus-related, and behavioural data are synchronized within the EEG data files for easy access and analysis. Technical validation confirmed data integrity, with spectral and physiological analyses showing responses associated with stimulus intensity and subjective pain/unpleasantness levels. By providing multimodal physiological data across painful and non-painful aversive conditions, this initiative represents a valuable resource for developing or validating biomarkers and exploring the multidimensional nature of pain perception.

pending_articles.title: Bone Marrow-Derived Cells Fuse with Bergmann Glia in Experimental Autoimmune Encephalomyelitis
pending_articles.content: Bone marrow-derived cells (BMDCs) can infiltrate the brain and adopt new identities through transdifferentiation or fusion, yet their interactions with specific neural cells remain poorly defined. We examined BMDC fusion with Bergmann glia (BG), a key cerebellar support cell, in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. After bone marrow transplantation, BMDCs fused with BG to form heterokaryons, retaining BG morphology and molecular markers. These heterokaryons contained donor and host nuclei that differed in both morphology and transcriptional activity. Remarkably, the BMDC nucleus localized not only to the soma but also along BG processes. This discovery identifies BMDC-BG fusion as a previously unrecognized form of glial plasticity, opening avenues for therapeutic strategies aimed at potentiating glial-mediated repair.

recently_processed.title: Closed-head injury produces a delayed, region-specific defect in glucose-carbon routing at the pyruvate branchpoint in APP/PS1 KI mice
recently_processed.content: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), and both conditions are associated with impaired glucose metabolism and mitochondrial dysfunction. We previously reported time-dependent mitochondrial dysfunction following closed-head injury (CHI) in amyloid precursor protein/presenilin 1 (APP/PS1) knock-in (KI) mice, but whether glucose-derived carbon labeling showed a corresponding temporal pattern remained unknown. We hypothesized that early deficits would involve tricarboxylic acid (TCA)-cycle metabolites, whereas chronic changes persisted upstream at the pyruvate-lactate branchpoint. Here, oral uniformly 13C-labeled glucose ([U-13C]-glucose) tracing and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS)-based isotopologue analysis were used to quantify first-turn glucose-derived carbon fate in cortex and hippocampus. To distinguish the effects of age at injury from those of post-injury interval, mice were analyzed 1 month after injury either at 7 or 12 months of age or 8 months after injury at 12 months of age. The most pronounced alterations occurred 8 months after CHI, when KI mice exhibited increased pyruvate and lactate labeling in the cortex and broader increases in glycolytic labeling in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that in APP/PS1 KI mice, chronic closed-head injury produced a delayed shift in glucose-derived carbon labeling centered on glycolytic and pyruvate/lactate nodes, with loss of hippocampal precursor-product coupling but without broad reduction of first-turn TCA-linked labeling.

recently_processed.title: Hormonal factors are poor indicators of endometriosis pain
recently_processed.content: Endometriosis is a common yet understudied condition in which sex hormones play a key role in the etiology and pathophysiology of the disease. Sex hormones are dysregulated in endometriosis and are pharmacologically targeted to reduce symptoms including pain, but the relationships between endometriosis-related pain with sex hormone levels and their receptors are not clear. In 60 women previously diagnosed or undergoing laparoscopic surgery for the diagnosis of endometriosis, we collected patient-reported endometriosis/pelvic pain intensity in the last 30 days, pain interference scale, and the Endometriosis Health Profile 30 (EHP30) pain subscale. In a sub-sample of 38 participants, biopsies from control non-lesion pelvic peritoneum and endometrial lesion tissues were collected during surgery to analyze the tissue abundance of the primary receptors for estrogen, as well as androgen, progesterone, and prolactin receptors. Serum was collected to analyze systemic sex hormone levels including estradiol, prolactin, progesterone, and testosterone. Between tissues, we found elevated transcript levels for estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1) in lesions, but no difference in estrogen receptor beta (ESR2) transcript levels between tissue samples were found. Relating tissue receptor transcript levels to clinical pain revealed that only ESR1 and PGR in lesions were negatively associated with endometriosis/pelvic pain intensity, however, following false discovery rate correction the association with ESR1 was no longer statistically significant. No other tissue or systemic factors were associated with clinical pain outcomes. Together, these data demonstrate unique alterations in receptor abundance in lesions yet select transcript levels only weakly relate to pain in endometriosis.

recently_processed.title: The potato cyst nematode Globodera pallida possesses an expanded serotonergic nervous system
recently_processed.content: Abstract The neurotransmitter serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) controls behaviours that are essential for the parasitic lifestyle of plant parasitic nematodes (PPNs). Here, we used serotonin immunochemistry and in situ hybridization for the serotonin synthesis genes, Gpa-tph-1 and Gpa-bas-1, to map its signalling pathways in Globodera pallida J2 infective stages. We identified fourteen serotonin-immunoreactive cell bodies around the pharyngeal median bulb and revealed that eleven of them co-express Gpa-tph-1 and Gpa-bas-1, confirming these are serotonin-synthesising neurons. Serotonin immunoreactivity was also localised in structures consistent with labelling of amphids, and in sixteen non-neuronal cells located in the middle and posterior region of the nematode. Depletion of serotonin with reserpine reduced the serotonin immunoreactivity in all fourteen cell bodies confirming their neuronal identity, but not in non-neuronal tissue. We identified additional, but infrequent expression of Gpa-tph-1 in two cells and expression of Gpa-bas-1 in one pair of symmetrically bilateral cells anterior to the median bulb, that lacked serotonin immunoreactivity. The results reveal distinct pools of serotonin distribution in G. pallida and indicate serotonin signalling is more complex than in other parasitic nematodes and C. elegans, highlighting evolutionary divergence in neurotransmitter identity.

recently_processed.title: Successor representation supports structural learning of syllable sequences
recently_processed.content: Humans efficiently learn the temporal structure of speech, yet the underlying cognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Recent research in visuospatial sequential memory has proposed the successor representation (SR), important in reinforcement learning, which encodes multi-step transitional relationships. To test whether SR also supports the structural learning of rapidly changing speech syllable sequences, we adapted a pyramid-structured sequential learning paradigm using syllable streams presented at a natural speech rate (~ 4 Hz). Participants exhibited robust structural learning, evidenced by asymmetric memory performance modulated by adjacent transitional probabilities. Notably, the SR model captured recognition performance for non-adjacent syllable pairs. Moreover, SR-based learning effects generalized across all syllable sequences, regardless of adjacency. Furthermore, the effectiveness of SR learning was associated with cognitive flexibility and working memory capacity. Together, these findings suggest that humans rely on effortful SR-like mechanisms for the structural learning of syllable sequences, highlighting a modality-general computational principle for sequential learning across various temporal modulation scales.
recently_processed.author: Liu, J., Wang, Y., Feng, J., Zhao, H., He, Q., Yang, X., Liang, B.

recently_processed.title: Latent dentate gyrus engrams formed in infancy scaffold adult learning
recently_processed.content: Infantile amnesia refers to the loss of event-based memories acquired early in life. In mice, however, these memories are not erased; selective optogenetic stimulation of engrams formed in infancy leads to memory recovery in adulthood, indicating that infant-formed engrams can persist in a latent form. We therefore asked whether these latent engrams, although not accessible through natural retrieval, nonetheless influence related adult learning. Using a contextual fear conditioning paradigm, we find that adult learning is facilitated by prior experience in infancy, both for the same and related contexts. Activity-dependent engram tagging revealed that adult learning reactivates infant-acquired dentate gyrus ensembles, and selective inactivation of these ensembles during adulthood abolished this facilitation. These findings indicate that memories formed in infancy persist as latent engrams that scaffold subsequent learning, consistent with a role in establishing schema-like representations.
